title: Bitcoin sellers make a play below the range. Can they keep control?
summary: Last week, the bitcoin buyers had their shot. On Tuesday, they pushed the price above the 100- and 200-hour moving averages—the blue and green lines—and that break gave them the technical go-ahead to probe higher. The buying subsequently took the price above the ceiling near $84,178 and to a weekly high of $84,774 on Wednesday. That was the opportunity for the buyers to take more control. They had cleared the hourly moving averages and broken above a familiar resistance level. The next step was to hold those breaks and build on the upside momentum. They could not do it. The price rotated lower as risk-off sentiment weighed on bitcoin. On Thursday, the decline took the price back below the 100- and 200-hour moving averages, then near $82,225 and $82,400. The bullish technical picture from earlier in the week shifted back in favor of the sellers. The failed rebound helped confirm the shift On Friday, the price bounced back toward the 200-hour moving average, but sellers leaned against that level and pushed the price lower into the weekend. That retest is an important part of the technical story. A break below a moving average is an initial bearish development. When the price subsequently returns to that moving average and finds sellers, it provides additional evidence that traders are using the level to define resistance and risk. title: UK autumn budget preview: Can Healey calm markets and change BOE rate hike bets?
summary: The UK autumn budget is coming up on 28 October, just a week before the BOE's next monetary policy decision . And with inflation concerns still hanging over the economy , the government's fiscal plans could have a say in how interest rate expectations develop over the coming months. For now, traders are pricing in roughly 99% odds of a 25 bps rate hike at the November meeting next week. So unless something really unexpected happens, that decision looks pretty much settled. As for December though, that is another story. Traders are currently pricing in around 47% odds of another rate hike before the year is out. That's essentially a coin toss and the autumn budget could be one to help tip expectations one way or the other. So, what should traders be looking out for? For starters, the general expectation is for a fairly cautious budget - one with modest tax increases and targeted support for households rather than any major spending commitments. The backdrop is one where the government's fiscal headroom is looking rather uncomfortable. According to EY, that buffer against the government's fiscal rules has shrunk from £23.6 billion in March to an estimated £11.3 billion. That is largely because of higher borrowing costs and the economic fallout from the Iran conflict. The latest Reuters survey suggests that Healey should try and rebuild that buffer to around £15-16 billion to reassure bond investors. So, that at least gives us some useful benchmark for judging the budget. On tax

The latter is the standout here and reaffirms a more resilient setting for the German economy, even though recent PMI data has revealed some underlying weakness. Still, the survey numbers here are not exactly hard data. So, we will have to see how this eventually transforms to the actual economic numbers in the months ahead to have a better sense of how well the economy might be holding up. The data won't do much to change the ECB decision this week though but we'll see how it fits among the trend in other data releases before the December meeting. title: The cost of intelligence is collapsing
summary: OpenAI is just out with a new model named GPT 6.1 Terra. This isn't as strong as GPT-6 Astra but it's far more efficient and it gets to the heart of where AI is headed. AI is becoming a commodity faster than it is becoming an indispensable service. Already we have the Sol model, which is near Astra at a fifth of the price but now we have Terra, which cuts the price in half again. OpenAI also touts the model as being particularly useful for automated computer use. "Terra understands what’s on screen, takes action across apps, writes naturally, and is a more capable model for your whole workday with the efficiency to take on more of it." I'm skeptical of the 'writes naturally' claims from any of the models but there has been steady improvements across all tasks. For markets, falling costs make adoption more attractive, but they also raise questions about the margins and returns on capital of the companies supplying AI infrastructure. Ultimately, I strongly believe that all the benefits of AI will fall to incumbent asset-heavy companies that can use it to improve efficiency rather than model makers. Now the bulls will argue Jevon's Paradox and I think that can run for awhile (years) but models are getting so intelligent and cheap that soon they will have extremely cheap models that cover 99% of use cases.
